curriculumDefinition.commandsAndConcepts: `:s/pattern/replacement/flags`; line, numeric, visual, and `%` ranges; flags `g c i I n`; empty/reused pattern or replacement; alternate delimiters; `. * \+ \? \{m,n}`; `^ $`; classes and negation; Vim classes such as `\d`, `\w`, `\s`; groups `\(…\)`; alternation `\|`; word boundaries `\< \>`; captures; `\zs \ze`; very magic `\v`; replacement `&`, `\0`–`\9`, `\r`, case conversion, and `\=` expressions
curriculumDefinition.learningOutcome: Perform safe local and buffer-wide substitutions, capture structure, preview impact, and know when regex is too brittle
curriculumDefinition.representativeExercises: Rename exact tokens; swap captured fields; edit only part of a match; normalize declarations; confirm replacements; count matches without changing them
curriculumDefinition.priorityAndPortability: Core through captures and confirmation. `\zs`, `\ze`, case conversion, and expression replacement are advanced

activities.title: Scope, preview, then transform
activities.body: You can now build local and ranged substitutions, control case and repetition, preview or confirm impact, and capture practical text structure. Keep patterns narrow, inspect broad edits, and switch tools when text matching becomes brittle.
takeaways: Ranges select lines; patterns select text within them.
Use `n` to preview and `c` when matches need judgment.
Advanced syntax does not make a brittle regex safe.

reference.purpose: Read and execute the pattern, replacement, delimiter, and range as one Ex command.
notes: `:s/pattern/replacement/flags` searches the addressed lines, replaces matching text, and applies optional flags. Without a range, it acts only on the current line.

reference.purpose: Apply substitutions to the current line, numeric ranges, Visual selections, and the whole buffer.
notes: The same substitution can act on one line, a numeric range, a Visual range, or `%` for the whole buffer. A narrow range is easier to predict and review.

reference.purpose: Distinguish one match from all matches and choose explicit case behavior.
notes: `g` replaces every match on each addressed line. `i` ignores case for this command, while `I` forces case-sensitive matching.

reference.purpose: Count impact before editing and make deliberate per-match confirmation decisions.
notes: The `n` flag reports how many matches would be affected without changing text. The `c` flag pauses at each match for `y`, `n`, `a`, `q`, or `l`.

reference.purpose: Reuse search and substitution history while keeping delimiter-heavy commands readable.
notes: An empty pattern reuses the latest search pattern. An empty replacement deletes matches. Alternate delimiters such as `#` avoid escaping `/` in paths and URLs.

reference.purpose: Use anchors, classes, negation, quantifiers, and Vim character classes without turning the lesson into a general regex course.
notes: Vim patterns use `.`, `*`, escaped quantifiers such as `\+`, `\?`, and `\{m,n}`, anchors `^` and `$`, bracket classes, negation, and classes such as `\d`, `\w`, and `\s`.

reference.purpose: Use grouping, alternation, boundaries, captures, whole matches, and line breaks in replacements.
notes: Vim groups use `\(…\)`, alternation uses `\|`, and `\<`/`\>` mark word boundaries. Replacements can reuse the whole match with `&` or `\0`, captures with `\1`–`\9`, and create a line break with `\r`.

reference.purpose: Apply very-magic and match-boundary tools, then recognize when regex is the wrong mechanism.
notes: `\v` makes most punctuation special. `\zs` starts the replaced portion inside a larger match, and `\ze` ends it early. Vim also supports replacement case conversion and `\=` expressions; those are advanced reference topics and are not executable in Vim Wilds yet.
